title: Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits
one_liner: A database and paid inspection report that rates shuttered Midwest plants on the things reshoring manufacturers actually need (utility service, slab, crane, transferable air and discharge permits) instead of square footage.
customer: Reshoring manufacturers and their site-selection consultants (first buyer). Industrial listing brokers and sellers of dead factories (they pay to differentiate their listings). Regional economic-development bodies and utility economic-development teams (annual license).
problem: Brokers list buildings by square feet, clear height and dock doors. A reshoring plant needs enough energized 480V/13.2kV capacity, a slab that can carry presses and large CNCs, crane rails, and a transferable Ohio EPA air permit for a paint or wash line. Greenfield permitting and long-lead transformers and switchgear can add 9-18 months before the first good part. Meanwhile data-center developers are hunting the same brownfield shells for their existing utility service, so the buildings that suit manufacturing are disappearing without either side understanding what was in them.
solution: Build a parcel-level dataset of pre-2005 industrial buildings across Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Indiana by combining public air and wastewater permit records, county parcel data, utility maps, aerial imagery for crane bays and rail spurs, and Phase I history. Score each building on power, permits, structure and contamination risk. Sell a 'Power Passport': a 12-page report with a licensed industrial electrician's walk-through, gear nameplate photos, permit transferability notes and utility will-serve context, delivered in 5 days.
why_now: The 2026 reshoring wave and the data-center land grab are competing for the same shells. Transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in many months to years. The gap between what manufacturers need and what listings say is at its widest, and brokers have no tooling to fill it.
revenue_model: $1.5k-$3.5k per Passport (paid by the broker or seller, or by the buyer). A 0.5%-1% success fee on closed industrial deals. $25k-$60k per year data licences to economic-development agencies, utilities and site-selection firms. Later, a capital vehicle that buys the best shells and subdivides them into permitted multi-tenant 'factory condos'.
non_obvious_insight: In a dead Ohio plant the building is the cheapest part. The energized service, the paper permits and the crane rails are the asset, and they are invisible to anyone who has not tried to open a factory. Every reshorer I know lost most of a year to power and permits, not to hiring.
first_30_days: Pick one metro (Akron/Canton or the Mahoning Valley). Pull public Ohio EPA permit records and county parcel data to list 150 candidate buildings. Hire an electrician for 20 walk-throughs at about $150 per hour. Cold-call 25 industrial listing brokers offering a free first Passport in exchange for a testimonial and a right to the data. Convert 3-5 into paying $1.5k reports and one economic-development office into a pilot licence.

tournament.cluster: US machine shops and reshoring manufacturers
judge_notes: contrarian: rank 1/25 - Insider insight (energized service and permits are the asset) is right; data-center shell scramble makes it timely and quick to test.
vc: rank 3/25 - Energized capacity and permits as the asset is non-obvious; data-center shell competition widens the buyer pool beyond reshorers.
operator: rank 4/25 - Real, ignored gap between listings and power and permits. $1.5k reports, an electrician and cold-calling brokers work in one metro.

competitors.name: Brownfield.ai
competitors.what_they_do: Site triage and listings platform for brownfield owners and buyers (advanced manufacturing, data centers, logistics). It scans environmental and property records and lists 'power availability' as the main screening factor for data-center buyers. The pages I read did not show building-level electrical verification, crane or slab data, or permit-transfer scoring.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Not disclosed on the pages I read; no funding or founder info found

competitors.name: Scout (ScoutCities)
competitors.what_they_do: Industrial site-selection platform for manufacturers. It surfaces off-market industrial real estate and incentives and lets users prioritise power, workforce and site specs. It claims a network of 10,000 economic developers and 25,000 brokers and site selectors. It appears to be desktop and network-based, with no per-building electrician walk-through that I could find.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Crunchbase shows a pre-seed round (amount not verified). The site returned 403, so the summary comes from search snippets.

competitors.name: LandGate
competitors.what_they_do: Parcel search with proprietary substation offtake-capacity data (about 98% coverage, 84,000+ substations), utility-upgrade cost analytics, and a PowerLeads land marketplace, aimed at data-center and industrial siting. Its data is grid- and substation-level, not inside-the-fence building gear. Brownfield features are not detailed.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established company, funding not confirmed; sold by quote

competitors.name: Enverus Site & Screen
competitors.what_they_do: Combines parcel data with grid, substation withdrawal-capacity and gas infrastructure. It is pitched at data-center, industrial and manufacturing site screening. It is an enterprise data product with no on-site inspection.

competitors.name: GridCARE
competitors.what_they_do: AI grid-capacity mapping and 'time to power' acceleration. It validates spare capacity with utilities for hyperscalers and 15+ data-center developers (2+ GW across a dozen markets).
competitors.scale_or_funding: $64M Series A (May 2026, led by Sutter Hill Ventures), after a $13.5M seed

competitors.name: Paces
competitors.what_they_do: YC-backed software that unifies grid, permitting, zoning and environmental data to find viable sites. It started with renewables and is expanding to EV charging and data centers.
competitors.scale_or_funding: $11M Series A (2024), plus pre-seed and YC funding

competitors.name: JobsOhio SiteOhio / Ohio Site Inventory Program
competitors.what_they_do: State-run database of 7,300+ properties. SiteOhio authentication verifies utility capacity, environmental studies and agency concurrence, but focuses on 30+ acre sites rather than the electrical, crane or slab specs of existing buildings. The evaluation is free, with a $500 fee only if a site is authenticated.
competitors.scale_or_funding: State-funded via JobsOhio; effectively a free substitute for part of the data

competitors.name: AEP and FirstEnergy economic-development site and building databases
competitors.what_they_do: Utility-run searchable databases of sites and move-in-ready buildings. AEP 'featured sites' are vetted for ample electric capacity and voltage. FirstEnergy has a comparable database: https://firstenergycorp.com/content/fecorp/economicdevelopment/site_location_services/sites_and_buildings.html. They are free and are also the likely licensees or channel partners. I could not confirm whether they list building-level gear.

competitors.name: ZoomProspector (Future Thinking Locations)
competitors.what_they_do: The licensed site and building database that many economic-development organisations and utilities embed (AEP Prospector, state Prospectors). It is the incumbent distribution channel for the 'annual license' buyer, but it is a listings and demographics tool, not an inspected-attribute dataset.

competitors.name: Site Selection Group and other site-selection consultants (Cushman & Wakefield, BLS Strategies)
competitors.what_they_do: Custom advisory work that says power is now 'the starting point' and tells clients to evaluate existing service, utilisation and incremental capacity. No productised building database was described in the article. The firms could add this as a service line, or become customers.

competitors.name: Property Condition Assessment and electrical inspection firms
competitors.what_they_do: Commodity alternative. An ASTM E2018 PCA already has to state service ampacity, voltage and phase, and buyers can hire a commercial electrician pre-purchase. This is the workaround customers use today; it is bespoke, unscored and not tied to permits or a database.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Fragmented local engineering and inspection firms

competition.white_space: Nobody I found productises a building-level, physically verified 'inside-the-fence' record for dead Midwest plants. That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The genuine gap is a trusted, standardised, seller-commissioned building electrical and permit record, not the parcel-scoring layer, which is already crowded and funded. The idea's weaker points: the Ohio permit-transferability wedge is thin (see evidence), and it is unproven that brokers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k.
competition.evidence_of_demand:
Partial evidence only. I found no RFPs, forum threads or existing broker spend on this specific product.

Supporting evidence:
- Power is now a lead site-selection criterion. Site Selection Group says 'power availability, upgrade timelines, and utility costs have become the starting point' for manufacturers (https://info.siteselectiongroup.com/blog/why-power-availability-is-altering-manufacturing-site-selection). Similar pieces: Voit (https://voitco.com/access-to-power-the-new-priority-for-industrial-site-selection/), Link Logistics (https://www.linklogistics.com/news-insights/industry-expertise/power-capacity-in-warehouse-site-selection/), JLL (https://www.jll.com/en-us/newsroom/power-availability-becoming-key-driver-of-cre-value), and Utility Dive on power-ready facilities (https://www.utilitydive.com/news/big-power-ready-facilities-key-as-occupiers-drive-industrial-market-improv/822244/).
- Equipment lead times are long. Large transformers average about 128 weeks (https://syaala.com/blog/transformer-lead-times-2026). Switchgear runs about 44 weeks on average and 90+ in some markets (https://usevawn.com/resources/electrical-equipment-lead-times/).
- Undersized service is a common post-lease surprise, with upgrades of about 3-9 months and $50k-$500k+ (WareCRE-style industrial spec guidance, https://warecre.com/cre-insights/industrial-101/loading-docks-ceiling-heights-and-power-requirements-understanding-industrial-property-specs/; attribution is from a search snippet and not verified).
- Customers already pay for power-availability reports. SCE sells an Engineering Analysis Report for about $3,000 covering power availability and time to build infrastructure (https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/utilities-and-site-selection-a-powerful-partnership/). The price sits inside your $1.5k-$3.5k band, but it is a utility-issued report, not a broker-paid one.
- Investors are paying for the adjacent data layer: GridCARE's $64M Series A (https://www.latitudemedia.com/news/gridcare-raises-oversubscribed-64-million-series-a/) and Paces' $11M Series A.
- Data centers are competing for existing energized industrial shells. Akron's former Goodyear plant now runs about 150 MW (https://signalakron.org/where-7-data-centers-operate-in-summit-county-and-why-it-matters/). TeraWulf and Anthropic signed a $19B lease on a shuttered aluminum plant (https://www.constructionaibrief.com/posts/2026-07-08-terawulf-anthropic-brownfield-aluminum-plant-data-center). Host Digital Infrastructure has a 45+ MW converted facility (https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/09/03/3356181/0/en/the-scarcest-thing-in-the-ai-buildout-is-a-site-that-already-has-power.html). Bisnow: https://www.bisnow.com/national/news/data-center/brownfield-data-centers-109798.

Counter-evidence:
- The 2026 Reshoring Initiative survey coverage I retrieved names workforce (66% rate technician hiring very difficult or crisis) and policy uncertainty (57% of OEMs) as the main challenges, and does not mention power or permitting (https://www.qualitymag.com/articles/99902-new-survey-us-reshoring-momentum-builds-despite-policy-and-workforce-challenges). The founder's claim that reshorers lose a year to power and permits is not backed by that survey.
- Ohio EPA guidance says an ownership transfer needs only a notification letter within 30 days, and no permit modification unless the new owner requests one (https://epa.ohio.gov/static/Portals/27/eBusinessCenter/Agency/DAPC/GUIDANCE_tranownership.doc). Idle facilities can keep permits if fees and reports stay current. That makes 'transferable permit' real but easy to check, so the permit component is a weaker moat than the power component.
- Ohio has 125+ data-center moratoriums (https://www.mahoningmatters.com/news/state/article317296239.html). That may ease competition for shells locally, but it also weakens the 'disappearing shells' urgency in Ohio.
competition.sharper_angle:
Change who pays and drop the parts that are already crowded. Do not sell a scoring database to manufacturers, because LandGate, Enverus, Scout, Brownfield.ai and ZoomProspector cover parcel scoring and search. Sell an 'Electrical and Permit As-Built Record' to sellers and controllers of idle plants. That means bankruptcy trustees and liquidators, corporate real-estate divisions, county land banks, port and development authorities, and utility economic-development teams. They have a direct financial reason to prove a building's energized capacity, and the record supports a powered-shell premium.

1. Core deliverable: the electrician-verified one-line diagram, nameplates, gear age and condition, spare capacity, and a utility will-serve or capacity letter. Add slab and crane-rail condition and the state of the existing air and wastewater permits (shutdown status, fee and renewal compliance). Sell it as a standardised, dual-use record that both a manufacturer and a data-center, battery or powered-shell buyer can underwrite. The record then serves both buyer types instead of betting on the poorer one.
2. Channel: license the verified data as a white-label layer to AEP, FirstEnergy, JobsOhio and ZoomProspector-style databases. They list buildings but do not verify what is inside them.
3. Lead generation: use public Ohio EPA permit and parcel data to find idle plants and offer the seller a first record.
4. Drop the 0.5%-1% success fee. It likely needs a real-estate broker licence and creates conflicts with the seller-paid, buyer-trusted record. Charge per record and per data license instead.
5. Validate before building: get 5 sellers or liquidators to pre-pay for a record, and confirm that brokers or sellers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k. I found no evidence yet that they will.
